**Washington, D.C. –**U.S. News & World Report, the global authority in rankings and consumer advice, today announced the [2025 Best Jobs](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/rankings). The rankings offer a look at the best jobs across 17 categories – from sectors such as [technology](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/rankings/best-technology-jobs), [health care](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/rankings/best-healthcare-jobs), [business](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/rankings/best-business-jobs) and [creative services](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/rankings/best-creative-and-media-jobs) – to help job seekers at every level make the most informed career decisions. The rankings take into account the most important aspects of a job, including growth potential, work-life balance, job safety, employment rate and salary.

For the second consecutive year, the need for professionals in [health care](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/rankings/best-healthcare-jobs) roles resulted in Nurse Practitioner holding the No. 1 spot.

“Careers in health care and health care support continue to show promise in the 2025 rankings due to a steady need for medical professionals that aid in the health and well-being of the population,” says Carly Chase, vice president of Careers at U.S. News. “Nurse Practitioner maintains the No. 1 spot as this year’s best job because of its critical role in health management, the flexibility it provides and its strong 10-year career outlook.”

Following Nurse Practitioner in the overall ranking are IT Manager at No. 2, Physician Assistant at No. 3, Financial Manager at No. 4 and Software Developer at No. 5.

The 2025 job market currently reflects a hearty appetite for STEM-related fields as a whole, offering prospective job growth and high pay for many roles. STEM industries rank high among the [Best Jobs That Pay $100K or More](https://careers.usnews.com/advice/slideshows/25-best-jobs-that-pay-more-than-100k), with these industries holding 18 of the top 25 careers.

“Financial comfort and freedom are goals for many job seekers, with some aiming to one day earn more than six figures in their careers,” says Chase. “‘The Best Jobs that Pay 100K or More’ offers options to job-seekers who may not be aware of specific roles with high-paying returns.”

The 2025 Best Jobs rankings offer job seekers information on training and education requirements, median salary and job satisfaction across diverse sectors, including [social services](http://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/rankings/best-social-services-jobs), [education](http://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/rankings/best-education-jobs) and [construction](http://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/rankings/best-construction-jobs). [Best Jobs Without a College Degree](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/rankings/best-jobs-without-a-college-degree) and [Highest Paying Jobs Without a Degree](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/rankings/highest-paying-jobs-without-a-degree) are also offered for those who did not attend or finish college.

To determine the Best Jobs, U.S. News draws data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics to identify jobs with the greatest hiring demand. Jobs are then scored using five component measures: future prospects, wage potential, employment, job safety and stability, and work-life balance. For further details on how the rankings were calculated, see the [methodology](http://money.usnews.com/money/careers/articles/how-us-news-ranks-the-best-jobs/).

For more information, visit [Best Jobs](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/rankings/the-100-best-jobs) and share the rankings on [Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/usnewsandworldreport/), [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/company/us-news-and-world-report/posts/?feedView=all) and [X](https://twitter.com/usnews) using [#BestJobs](https://twitter.com/hashtag/bestjobs).

**Washington, D.C. –**U.S. News & World Report, the global authority in rankings and consumer advice, today announced the [2025 Best Jobs](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/rankings). The rankings offer a look at the best jobs across 17 categories – from sectors such as [technology](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/rankings/best-technology-jobs), [health care](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/rankings/best-healthcare-jobs), [business](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/rankings/best-business-jobs) and [creative services](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/rankings/best-creative-and-media-jobs) – to help job seekers at every level make the most informed career decisions. The rankings take into account the most important aspects of a job, including growth potential, work-life balance, job safety, employment rate and salary.

For the second consecutive year, the need for professionals in [health care](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/rankings/best-healthcare-jobs) roles resulted in Nurse Practitioner holding the No. 1 spot.

“Careers in health care and health care support continue to show promise in the 2025 rankings due to a steady need for medical professionals that aid in the health and well-being of the population,” says Carly Chase, vice president of Careers at U.S. News. “Nurse Practitioner maintains the No. 1 spot as this year’s best job because of its critical role in health management, the flexibility it provides and its strong 10-year career outlook.”

Following Nurse Practitioner in the overall ranking are IT Manager at No. 2, Physician Assistant at No. 3, Financial Manager at No. 4 and Software Developer at No. 5.

The 2025 job market currently reflects a hearty appetite for STEM-related fields as a whole, offering prospective job growth and high pay for many roles. STEM industries rank high among the [Best Jobs That Pay $100K or More](https://careers.usnews.com/advice/slideshows/25-best-jobs-that-pay-more-than-100k), with these industries holding 18 of the top 25 careers.

“Financial comfort and freedom are goals for many job seekers, with some aiming to one day earn more than six figures in their careers,” says Chase. “‘The Best Jobs that Pay 100K or More’ offers options to job-seekers who may not be aware of specific roles with high-paying returns.”

The 2025 Best Jobs rankings offer job seekers information on training and education requirements, median salary and job satisfaction across diverse sectors, including [social services](http://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/rankings/best-social-services-jobs), [education](http://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/rankings/best-education-jobs) and [construction](http://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/rankings/best-construction-jobs). [Best Jobs Without a College Degree](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/rankings/best-jobs-without-a-college-degree) and [Highest Paying Jobs Without a Degree](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/rankings/highest-paying-jobs-without-a-degree) are also offered for those who did not attend or finish college.

To determine the Best Jobs, U.S. News draws data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics to identify jobs with the greatest hiring demand. Jobs are then scored using five component measures: future prospects, wage potential, employment, job safety and stability, and work-life balance. For further details on how the rankings were calculated, see the [methodology](http://money.usnews.com/money/careers/articles/how-us-news-ranks-the-best-jobs/).

For more information, visit [Best Jobs](https://money.usnews.com/careers/best-jobs/rankings/the-100-best-jobs) and share the rankings on [Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/usnewsandworldreport/), [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/company/us-news-and-world-report/posts/?feedView=all) and [X](https://twitter.com/usnews) using [#BestJobs](https://twitter.com/hashtag/bestjobs).

Information technology managers, or computer and information systems managers, help organizations navigate the labyrinth of modern technology. These important employees have the responsibility of delivering short- and long-term visions for a company's technology needs and goals. Even though most IT managers have the technical chops to execute the various jobs of the workers they supervise, they are more likely to be spotted in a meeting room than a server room.   
  
Typical duties of an IT manager include coordinating with top executives, planning upgrades of existing software or hardware and negotiating with vendors for the service of current products or the purchase of new ones.   
  
IT managers also oversee the installation and maintenance of an organization's computer information systems, protecting the office network from hackers and malware.   
  
When the job is done well, many employees don't even notice the work involved. If you haven't had an email interruption or server meltdown in the past few months, you probably have an IT manager to thank.  
  
While the highest-profile jobs are in computer systems design, almost all organizations need IT managers, especially financial and insurance companies, manufacturing firms and the government. The growing health care industry is also expected to increase its information technology use, resulting in newly created positions. The chief growth drivers will be organizations upgrading their information technology systems to newer, faster networks and striving to avoid emerging cyberthreats. The Bureau of Labor Statistics projects 15.2% employment growth for it managers between 2024 and 2034. In that period, an estimated 101,600 jobs should open up.

## What is a Financial Manager?

![Image 5](https://www.usnews.com/dims4/USNEWS/d886d7a/2147483647/crop/417x274+0+0/resize/640x420/quality/85/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.usnews.com%2Fcmsmedia%2Fee%2F43ab15346528c1d9c064b606f89798%2Fjobs-job-photo-33.jpg)[Median Salary](https://careers.usnews.com/best-jobs/financial-manager#salary-overview)[$161,700](https://careers.usnews.com/best-jobs/financial-manager#salary-overview)Unemployment Rate 1.4%Number of Jobs 128,800

Financial managers oversee the finances of major companies, agencies and other organizations. Along with their teams, they coordinate accounting and produce financial reports, cash-flow statements and profit projections. ## What is a Pilot?

![Image 5](https://www.usnews.com/dims4/USNEWS/7d6084e/2147483647/thumbnail/640x420/quality/85/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.usnews.com%2Fcmsmedia%2Fed%2Fb5%2F67abbb164280bbb869f1011c6199%2Fpilotcockpit.jpg)[Median Salary](https://careers.usnews.com/best-jobs/pilot#salary-overview)[$226,600](https://careers.usnews.com/best-jobs/pilot#salary-overview)Unemployment Rate N/A Number of Jobs 3,900

Pilots fly and operate aircraft like airplanes and helicopters for airlines, private corporations, law enforcement agencies and the military. They also prepare the aircraft for flight, which includes ensuring there are no mechanical defects with the aircraft, verifying that scheduled maintenance is done and any repairs are complete, and checking the route of flight as well as departure, destination and alternate airports to make sure the flight is safe for weather conditions. Pilots also make sure the aircraft is properly balanced with passengers, cargo, baggage and fuel load.  
  
“You may be within your weight limitation, but if the balance is out, it can be very difficult to raise the nose or raise the tail if the center of gravity is off, just like on a teeter-totter,” says David Dornacker, flight simulator and academic ground school instructor at CAE USA, a major defense contractor that provides flight simulation training for the military. Dornacker was previously a pilot with ExpressJet Airlines (formerly Continental Express) for 14 years, where he served as first officer then captain, and prior to that was an air traffic controller with the U.S. Navy for 20 years.  
  
Getting the aircraft ready for takeoff is “not just a matter of loading up the aircraft and topping it off and going. You’ve got to actually have a plan; you have to know how much fuel you’re going to burn to get to your destination, you have to have reserve fuel left over to be compliant with federal air regulations, and should you need an alternate, you’ve got to have enough fuel to get to that alternate airport and then have adequate fuel reserves on board as well,” Dornacker says.  
  
Once preflight duties have been performed, pilots have the arduous job of getting the aircraft safely in the sky. Dornacker says the pilot files the route of flight, requests clearance from the air traffic controllers, takes position on the runway, runs through final checks for the aircraft, runs the power-up check on the engines, and then climbs out at the appropriate speed to get to the assigned cruising altitude.  
  
The Bureau of Labor Statistics groups pilots into two categories: airline and commercial. Airline pilots generally work on a fixed schedule for an airline as they transport people and cargo to their destinations. Commercial pilots typically perform unscheduled flights for corporations, wealthy individuals, aerial tours, charter flights and pesticide application.  
  
Ambulance services is expected to be a large area of growth among commercial pilots in the next decade, according to the BLS, as pilots will be hired to transport patients to hospitals and other health care facilities.   
  
The Bureau of Labor Statistics projects 3.9% employment growth for pilots between 2024 and 2034. In that period, an estimated 3,900 jobs should open up.

## How to Become a Pilot

A college degree isn’t a blanket requirement to become a pilot. But some airlines require a degree, so it’s recommended to give yourself the best choice of jobs in this field.   
  
Pilots receive a lot of on-the-job training, but Dornacker says, “normally, you get training from a scheduled operator trainer. There are Part 141 schools, which is a school that actually has a syllabus to it. They are moderate to expensive cost.”   
  
Military, college or civilian flight schools are the typical routes to becoming a pilot, says Shane Bise, first officer at NetJets, a private jet company based in Columbus, Ohio.   
  
“With college and civilian training, one typically starts as a student pilot and works up through their commercial pilot license,” says Bise, who is based in Cleveland.  
  
At that point, they have a few options. “Most go on to become flight instructors; however, some go on to tow banners in high tourist areas,” he says. “Sometimes, one can get lucky and find a smaller operator willing to give them a chance as a low-time pilot, but those opportunities are few and far between. After building up to between 1,000 and 1,500 hours (of actual pilot flying time), many more opportunities open up due to eligibility for the ATP license, which is the highest license available to a commercial pilot.”   
  
If a high salary is important to you, Dornacker says consider attending an aviation college, which could almost guarantee you a job after you graduate. That said, tuition and other fees could cost you well into the six figures.   
  
“It’s not very lucrative starting out because typically your first year, the salary is somewhere between the $30,000 and $50,000 range as a first officer,” he says. “As you get more senior with time, the better flying jobs come, and of course the better pay. The pay can exceed $350,000 a year now as a senior airline pilot at a place like FedEx, UPS or Delta.”   
  
If you’re considering a career as a pilot, Dornacker says you must pass a medical exam. “The first thing I would do before I put any serious money down in flight training is see if you can pass an Federal Aviation Administration Class 1 medical exam, because if you can’t, there’s no sense in spending any money on training. If you can hold a Class 2 medical but not a Class 1, at least you can become a corporate pilot. In order to work for a scheduled air carrier, you must have FAA Class 1 medical.”   
  
Pilots should also have strong math skills and a good grasp of mechanics, Bise says. “One skill that I think is often overlooked is customer service. … A pilot telling passengers what is causing a delay is such a small thing but goes a long way in conveying confidence and calmness to passengers, especially those who are nervous fliers.”  
  
Dornacker adds, “It’s good to be a good three-dimensional thinker because you’re operating in a three-dimensional environment. Let’s face it: We’re taking a very heavy aircraft/vehicle, putting it up at 37,000 feet at three-quarters the speed of sound, flying in pressurized, air-conditioned comfort. You’ve got to be able to tie all this stuff together and be a quick thinker when something does go amiss and have a solution to it.”  
  
In those quick-thinking situations, Dornacker says pilots primarily use the aircraft manuals to determine the appropriate fix and are only expected to have a few things memorized.   
  
While there’s no continuing education required as a pilot, Dornacker says, “you do have to prove yourself as an airline captain every six or nine months, depending on the air carrier and the FAA.”   
  
For that, you can expect to spend a couple days in ground school, which will cover any changes to rules and regulations, company policy updates and instruction in crew resource management. “After you do that, then you go off to the flight simulators.”
